doc.title: Charles Calello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 21, 2025

title: The Name Game, Sweet Caroline and changing instrumentation
summary: He explains baritone saxes and bass trombone as power chords on The Name Game and the Bee Gees instrumentation behind Sweet Caroline.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: That was a technique that I developed when I was doing “The Name Game.” What I did was I had two baritone saxes and a bass trombone play octaves and fifth – and a fifth. They were like musical power chords. And what was interesting about “The Name Game” if you listen to the record it’s sort of fun to analyze because the rhythm was like [scats] but the bass never played that. The bass played [scats]. So what happened was, with my short Schillinger education I learned that you could actually take different rhythms and make them work against one another. So while the low end was doing like [scats] they’re going [scats]. And then with the African drums and everything, it was such a cool record to make. So I had established all those sounds, and this became like sort of my staple orchestra at that time. It’s just like as the music changed the instrumentation changed. In the ‘70s, well after the ‘60s, when the music started to change, the orchestrations started to change. I started to listen to the Bee Gees records and when I did the arrangement to “Sweet Caroline” and wrote the bomp-bomp-bomp I took the instrumentation from a Bee Gees record. The Bee Gees were using two trumpets, two trombones and strings. And I thought that a lot of the songs that I was getting asked to arrange sounded like they fit the Bee Gee bag. So I started to use that instrumentation.
Later on as the types of music changed, the orchestrations would change. And how the records would be put together would be determined by the style and what was being played on the radio.
I believe I read that Neil Diamond gave you a sort of a wishy-washy compliment on your work for “Sweet Caroline.”
Yeah when I walked out of the studio I says, “How was that Neil?” He says, “Well I didn’t hear anything wrong with it.”
